entities.name: Fine Gael
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Fine Gael ('Family of the Irish'), founded in 1933 from the merger of Cumann na nGaedheal, the National Centre Party, and the Army Comrades Association (Blueshirts), is the senior partner of the 2020 coalition that ended Ireland's Civil War political divide — traditionally the more pro-European, pro-NATO, and economically liberal of Ireland's two main parties, with roots in the pro-Treaty side of the Irish Civil War (1922-1923). Fine Gael produced Ireland's most internationally significant Taoiseach in Garret FitzGerald (the Anglo-Irish Agreement, 1985) and governed through Ireland's economic recovery.

Fine Gael's predecessor Cumann na nGaedheal governed the Irish Free State 1922-1932, accepting the Anglo-Irish Treaty partition as a practical step toward full independence. The merger with the Blueshirts — a semi-fascist movement that sent volunteers to fight for Franco in Spain — created lasting reputational complications. Fine Gael positioned itself as the 'responsible' pro-market, pro-European party versus Fianna Fáil's protectionist nationalism.

Garret FitzGerald's Anglo-Irish Agreement (1985) — signed with Margaret Thatcher — gave the Irish government a formal consultative role in Northern Irish governance for the first time, breaking the post-partition political stalemate. The agreement's recognition of the Irish nationalist community's rights in Northern Ireland created the framework for the Good Friday Agreement (1998) that ended the Troubles. Enda Kenny's 2011-2016 government managed Ireland's EU-IMF bailout recovery, restoring creditworthiness and returning to growth.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Fine Gael's Anglo-Irish Agreement (1985) — giving the Irish government a formal role in Northern Ireland governance for the first time — created the political framework that made the 1998 Good Friday Agreement possible, ending the Troubles and achieving the peaceful partition settlement that shaped modern Ireland.
